rmt-2004-team-01.title: Square it
rmt-2004-team-01.body:
$(\sin x-\cos x)^2=1-\sin2x=\frac1{2003}$. For $\frac{5\pi}4<x<\frac{9\pi}4$ we have $\sin x-\cos x=\sqrt2\sin\left(x-\frac\pi4\right)$ with $x-\frac\pi4\in(\pi,2\pi)$, so it is negative. Hence $\sin x-\cos x=-\frac1{\sqrt{2003}}$.

**Answer: $-\frac1{\sqrt{2003}}$**

rmt-2004-team-02.title: Geometric series
rmt-2004-team-02.body:
A roll of two dice totals 6 with probability $\frac5{36}$ and totals 7 with probability $\frac16$. Dave wins on his first turn with $\frac5{36}$; otherwise (probability $\frac{31}{36}$) Daly must also fail (probability $\frac56$) and the game restarts. So $P=\frac5{36}+\frac{31}{36}\cdot\frac56P$, giving $P\left(1-\frac{155}{216}\right)=\frac5{36}$, i.e. $P=\frac{30}{61}$.

**Answer: $\frac{30}{61}$**

rmt-2004-team-03.title: Hexagon plus six triangles
rmt-2004-team-03.body:
The diagonals form a smaller regular hexagon in the middle (with side one third of the diagonal length, i.e. side $\frac s{\sqrt3}$ where $s$ is the side of $ABCDEF$), so its area is $\frac13$ of the big hexagon. The star is this inner hexagon together with six congruent equilateral triangles on its sides; folding these triangles over their common sides with the inner hexagon shows that their total area equals that of the inner hexagon. Hence the star has area $2\cdot\frac13=\frac23$. (Coordinates confirm the value $\frac23$.)

**Answer: $\frac23$**

rmt-2004-team-04.title: Check the last digits
rmt-2004-team-04.body:
We need $n^3\equiv n^2\pmod{100}$, i.e. $n^2(n-1)\equiv0\pmod{100}$. Mod 4 this holds iff $n$ is even or $n\equiv1\pmod4$. Mod 25 it holds iff $5\mid n$ or $n\equiv1\pmod{25}$. Combine: $n$ even and $5\mid n$: the multiples of 10, $10,20,\ldots,90$ (sum 450). $5\mid n$ and $n\equiv1\pmod4$: $n\equiv5\pmod{20}$, i.e. $25,45,65,85$ (sum 220). $n\equiv1\pmod{25}$ and $n$ even: $n\equiv26\pmod{50}$, i.e. $26,76$ (sum 102). $n\equiv1\pmod{25}$ and $n\equiv1\pmod4$ gives $n\equiv1\pmod{100}$, no two-digit values. Total $450+220+102=772$.

**Answer: 772**

rmt-2004-team-06.title: Count assignments
rmt-2004-team-06.body:
Only the set of seats occupied by the four Bobs matters: all $\binom{13}4=715$ sets of seats are equally likely (cars of sizes 4, 4, 5). Every car needs a Bob, so the Bobs split $2,1,1$ among the cars. Two Bobs in the 5-seater: $\binom52\cdot4\cdot4=160$ seat sets. Two Bobs in the first 4-seater: $\binom42\cdot4\cdot5=120$. Two Bobs in the second 4-seater: $120$. Total $400$, so the probability is $\frac{400}{715}=\frac{80}{143}$.

**Answer: $\frac{80}{143}$**

rmt-2004-team-07.title: Geometric series trick
rmt-2004-team-07.body:
For $|x|<1$, $\sum_{k\ge1}kx^k=\frac x{(1-x)^2}$ (equivalently $\left(\frac1{1-x}-1\right)\frac1{1-x}$). Setting $y=\frac1{1-x}$ gives $y(y-1)=20$, so $y=5$ or $y=-4$, i.e. $x=\frac45$ or $x=\frac54$. The series diverges for $x=\frac54$, so the only solution is $x=\frac45$.

**Answer: $x=\frac45$**

rmt-2004-team-08.title: Viviani's theorem
rmt-2004-team-08.body:
Join $P$ to the three vertices. The three small triangles have total area equal to the area of $ABC$: $\frac12\cdot2004\cdot d(P)=\frac{\sqrt3}4\cdot2004^2$, so $d(P)=\frac{\sqrt3}2\cdot2004$ is constant (the altitude). Hence $M=m$ and $M-m=0$.

**Answer: 0**

rmt-2004-team-09.title: Cycle structure of one round
rmt-2004-team-09.body:
Write out the permutation of one round and decompose it into cycles. Nine owls (positions 2, 8, 11, 12, 14, 18, 20, 24, 30) stay in place; the owls in spots 16 and 19 swap (a 2-cycle); four owls in spots 21, 23, 26, 28 form a 4-cycle; and the remaining 15 owls form a single 15-cycle. The order of the permutation is $\operatorname{lcm}(2,4,15)=60$. (A direct simulation of the three phases confirms 60.)

**Answer: 60**

rmt-2004-team-10.title: Pair x with -x
rmt-2004-team-10.body:
Let $F(x)=\lfloor2x^3-2\lfloor x^3\rfloor\rfloor$; it is $\lfloor2\{x^3\}\rfloor$, i.e. 0 if the fractional part of $x^3$ is below $\frac12$ and 1 otherwise. For $x^3$ not an integer or half-integer, $\{-x^3\}=1-\{x^3\}$, so exactly one of $F(x),F(-x)$ is 1: $F(x)+F(-x)=1$. Hence the average over the symmetric interval is $\frac12$. (Numerical integration agrees.)

**Answer: $\frac12$**

rmt-2004-team-11.title: Euler's totient
rmt-2004-team-11.body:
The grains in the second pile are those $n\le25!$ coprime to $25!$, i.e. to every prime $p\le23$. Their fraction is $\frac{\varphi(25!)}{25!}=\prod_{p\le23}\left(1-\frac1p\right)=\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac45\cdot\frac67\cdot\frac{10}{11}\cdot\frac{12}{13}\cdot\frac{16}{17}\cdot\frac{18}{19}\cdot\frac{22}{23}=\frac{110592}{676039}$.

**Answer: $\frac{110592}{676039}$**

rmt-2004-team-13.title: Integer roots summing to 5
rmt-2004-team-13.body:
A monic integer polynomial has only integer rational roots (rational root theorem), so the roots are four non-negative integers with sum 5 (the negative of the $x^3$ coefficient). The multisets are $\{0,0,0,5\}$, $\{0,0,1,4\}$, $\{0,0,2,3\}$, $\{0,1,1,3\}$, $\{0,1,2,2\}$, $\{1,1,1,2\}$: 6 of them. Each multiset determines the polynomial and hence $(b,c,d)$, and different multisets give different triples.

**Answer: 6**

rmt-2004-team-14.title: Pre-period of a fraction
rmt-2004-team-14.body:
The numerator $2004=2^2\cdot3\cdot167$ shares no factor with $7\cdot5^{2003}$, so the fraction is in lowest terms. The pre-period of the decimal expansion is the larger of the exponents of 2 and 5 in the denominator, here $\max(0,2003)=2003$ (and the period comes from the factor 7). Equivalently, by partial fractions $\frac A7+\frac B{5^{2003}}$: the first part is purely periodic and the second is a terminating decimal with exactly 2003 digits.

**Answer: 2003**

rmt-2004-team-15.title: Treat dice independently
rmt-2004-team-15.body:
Imagine each die is rolled separately in its own cup, $k$ times. A given die shows a six at least once in $k$ rolls with probability $1-\left(\frac56\right)^k$. All five dice have shown a six within $k$ rolls with probability $\left(1-\left(\frac56\right)^k\right)^5$, and this is the probability that the process finishes in at most $k$ rolls. Subtract the probability that it finishes in at most $k-1$ rolls to get exactly $k$ rolls.

**Answer: $\left(1-\left(\frac56\right)^k\right)^5-\left(1-\left(\frac56\right)^{k-1}\right)^5$**
